entries.en: The energy received per unit area depends on the angle of the Sun’s rays. Earth’s axial tilt of about 23.4° drives the seasons. The orbit is slightly elliptical, but distance from the Sun is not the cause of seasons. Land and ocean respond differently because water has a very high heat capacity.

Evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation and runoff cycle roughly 500,000 km³ of water through the atmosphere each year. Latent heat released by condensation powers storms. Water-holding capacity of air rises about 7% per °C (Clausius–Clapeyron relation).

Cloud droplets of about 10 µm grow by condensation and by collision and coalescence. In colder clouds the ice-crystal (Bergeron) process matters. Aerosols act as cloud condensation nuclei and influence droplet size.

Away from the equator, large-scale flow is close to geostrophic balance between the pressure-gradient and Coriolis forces. Near the equator the Coriolis effect is weak, which is why tropical cyclones rarely form within about 5° of it.

Relative humidity depends on temperature, so dew point or wet-bulb temperature is a better guide to heat stress. A wet-bulb temperature of 35 °C was long cited as the theoretical limit of human survival, and newer experiments suggest harm begins at lower values, especially for older people.

Charge separation involves collisions between graupel and ice crystals in the mixed-phase region of the cloud. A flash briefly heats the air to around 30,000 K. The 30-minute rule exists because lightning can strike well away from the rain core.
Water’s specific heat is about four times that of dry soil, and mixing in the upper ocean spreads heat through a deep layer. Sea-breeze fronts can trigger afternoon thunderstorms inland.

The monsoon is a seasonal reversal of low-level winds linked to the northward movement of the tropical rain belt (ITCZ), land–sea thermal contrast and heating of the Tibetan Plateau. Year-to-year variation is influenced by ENSO and the Indian Ocean Dipole. Observed trends include weaker June–September totals over parts of India and more frequent extreme-rain events.

Intensity depends on sea-surface temperature, ocean heat content, low vertical wind shear and mid-level moisture. IMD classes by maximum sustained wind: depression 17–27 knots, deep depression 28–33, cyclonic storm 34–47, severe cyclonic storm 48–63, very severe 64–89, extremely severe 90–119, super cyclonic storm 120 knots or more.

ENSO is tracked with the Oceanic Niño Index, a three-month mean sea-surface temperature anomaly in the Niño 3.4 region, with thresholds of ±0.5 °C. The Indian Ocean Dipole can strengthen or offset ENSO’s influence on Indian rainfall.

IMD heatwave departures are 4.5–6.4 °C above normal, and severe heatwave is more than 6.4 °C above normal. Absolute thresholds also apply, for example 45 °C or more. Heat illness risk depends on temperature, humidity, radiation, wind and individual health, so thresholds are guides rather than guarantees.

Risk is commonly framed as hazard × exposure × vulnerability. Urban flooding is driven by short, intense rainfall that exceeds drainage capacity, by sealed surfaces, and by lost natural storage in wetlands and tanks.

Indices such as SPI (precipitation), SPEI (which includes evapotranspiration) and soil-moisture anomalies track drought. Meteorological drought in India is typically flagged when seasonal rainfall is more than 25% below normal.

In deep water a tsunami travels at about 700–800 km/h with wavelengths of tens to hundreds of kilometres. Storm surge is a wind-driven rise of the sea surface, and its height adds to the astronomical tide to give the storm tide.

Doubling CO₂ gives a radiative forcing of about 4 W/m². Equilibrium climate sensitivity, the long-run warming for doubled CO₂, is assessed as likely between 2.5 and 4 °C with a best estimate of 3 °C (IPCC AR6).

Evidence includes CO₂ rising from about 280 ppm before industry to above 420 ppm, the isotopic signature of fossil carbon, ocean heat uptake, shrinking ice, and the fingerprint of tropospheric warming with stratospheric cooling, which a brighter Sun would not produce.
Observed global mean rise accelerated from about 1.3 mm per year (1901–1971) to 1.9 (1971–2006) and 3.7 mm per year (2006–2018), according to IPCC AR6.

Bleaching is expected when sea temperature exceeds the local summer maximum by about 1 °C for several weeks, tracked as degree heating weeks. Rising CO₂ also acidifies seawater, which makes it harder for shell-building and reef-building organisms to form their skeletons.

Ice-albedo feedback amplifies Arctic warming. Glacier retreat first increases river flow and later reduces it once the ice store is depleted, so water planning must account for a peak followed by decline.
Assessments by WMO and UNEP project the ozone layer returning to 1980 values around 2040 over most of the world, around 2045 over the Arctic and around 2066 over Antarctica.
Urban heat-island intensity is largest at night under calm, clear skies. It is distinct from greenhouse-driven warming and adds to it for city residents.

Fossil fuels and industry account for roughly nine-tenths of recent anthropogenic CO₂ emissions and land-use change for about one-tenth. About 45 to 50 percent of emitted CO₂ stays in the air, and the rest is taken up by land and ocean sinks, which could weaken in a warmer world.

Short-range forecasts rely on numerical models that solve atmospheric equations on a grid and assimilate observations from satellites, radars and stations. Skill falls with lead time because the atmosphere is chaotic. Nowcasts for the next 0 to 3 hours are the most reliable guide for thunderstorms.

Pathways limiting warming to 1.5 °C require global CO₂ emissions to fall by about 45% from 2010 levels by 2030 and reach net zero around 2050 (IPCC SR1.5). Maladaptation occurs when an action raises long-term risk or shifts harm to another group or place.
Warnings reach boats and fields. Needs phones, sirens and practice.
A safe building plus volunteers to carry those who cannot walk.
Slow and costly per house, but protects those with the least.
Water leaves faster, so fewer homes and fields stay flooded.
Softens waves and floods and shelters fish. Takes years to work.
Families recover faster, so one bad season does not become a crisis.
Cuts emissions and bills. One village cannot change the global hazard, so the effect here is tiny. It only matters if many places act.
India’s average surface temperature rose by roughly 0.7 °C between 1901 and 2018, and heatwaves have become more frequent in many regions (MoES 2020 assessment).
Cities add their own heat. Childhood summers are often remembered outdoors, while today’s heat may be felt indoors.
Ask three people of different ages. Then compare with the IMD record for your nearest station.
Night-time temperatures have been rising in many regions, and warmer air can hold more moisture, which makes heat feel stickier.
Concrete roofs hold heat after dark in a way thatched roofs did not. City heat-island effects add to the change.
Compare how your house type and the buildings around it have changed since childhood.

Studies report weaker June–September rainfall over parts of India since the mid-20th century, with more erratic spells. Tamil Nadu depends heavily on the October–December north-east monsoon, which swings strongly between years.
A few very wet or very dry years dominate memory.
Ask which specific years people remember, then look up the rainfall for those years.
Heavy-rain events have increased in many parts of India, consistent with warmer air holding about 7% more moisture for each 1 °C of warming.
Blocked drains, filled wetlands and paved ground make the same rain feel far worse.
Look for local reports of daily rainfall above 100 mm, and walk your street after rain to see where water stands.
Climate affects rainfall and recharge, but in most villages pumping, borewells, silted tanks and land-use change dominate groundwater trends.
Everyone may agree the water table fell, yet the main cause is often how much is pumped out.
Count borewells now versus in your elder’s youth. Ask when the village tank was last desilted.
Global sea level rose about 20 cm between 1901 and 2018, and the rise is speeding up. Local erosion also depends strongly on harbours, sand mining, reduced river sediment, mangrove loss and cyclones.
Do not mix up the 2004 tsunami, which was caused by an earthquake, with climate-driven change.
Ask where the old shoreline was, then compare with a map or satellite view and note any harbour or sea-wall built nearby.
Rainfall variability and ocean warming can shift crops and fish, but irrigation, seed varieties, prices, fleet size and overfishing change yields too.
Better boats and seeds can hide a climate effect, and worse markets can exaggerate one.
Ask what changed in the way they fish or farm, not only in the results.
Habitat loss, pesticides, night lighting and urban growth are major drivers of bird and insect declines. Climate adds pressure but is rarely the only cause.
Many people report a decline here. Shared experience is not proof of one cause.
Count the species you can find in 15 minutes near the home. Ask what was built, sprayed or lit up nearby.
Cold nights and mornings have become less frequent in many regions as average temperatures rose.
Trees, buildings and open ground change how cold a particular spot feels.
Compare minimum temperatures at the nearest IMD station for recent and older decades.

North Indian Ocean cyclones show no clear long-term rise in number, but the strongest storms and heavy rainfall are intensifying, and higher seas worsen storm surge. Floods also follow lost drainage and building on floodplains.
Notable storms are remembered; exposure has grown as more people live near the coast.
List the storms your elder names with years, then count how many people and houses were in harm’s way then versus now.
About 91% (IPCC AR6).
The ocean is the planet’s heat store. That is why seas rise as water expands, and why marine heatwaves matter.
About 430 ppm, rising by roughly 2–3 ppm a year. Check NOAA’s live figure.
The rise is far faster than natural changes recorded in ice cores, and its carbon signature points to fossil fuels.
About 1.1 °C for 2011–2020 (IPCC AR6). Recent single years have been higher.
A small change in a global average moves the whole distribution of weather, including the hot tail.
Roughly −18 °C (a standard textbook estimate).
The greenhouse effect is natural and essential. Climate change is about strengthening it.
About 7% (Clausius–Clapeyron relation).
This is one reason heavy downpours intensify in a warmer world.
About 20 cm (IPCC AR6).
It sounds small, yet it raises storm-surge reach and floods low coasts far more often.
About 0.7 °C for 1901–2018 (MoES 2020 assessment).
Regional change differs from the global figure, so local records still matter.
Close to zero, about −0.1 to +0.1 °C (IPCC AR6).
Natural factors push climate around, but they do not explain the sustained rise.
